Compression of the oculomotor nerve

Weakened muscle, relaxed tissues

That is myasthenia gravis.

A.io: e — Clinical skills for a complete and focused skin examination
A.q: Why is natural light preferred for inspecting the skin?

The concern is colour rendition rather than apparent size.
Natural light reduces the glare produced by moist lesions
Glare is not the stated problem with artificial light.
Artificial light may distort skin tone
Correct — the distortion can conceal jaundice, pallor and subtle erythema.
Natural light is brighter than any artificial source available in clinic
Brightness is not the reason; fidelity of colour is.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: Besides senile and congenital forms, which three causes of ptosis are there?
opts: Bell palsy, trigeminal neuralgia and stroke
Bell palsy weakens lid CLOSURE, not elevation.
Thyroid eye disease, orbital cellulitis and tumour
Those cause proptosis, which is a different finding.
Blepharitis, chalazion and dermatochalasis
Those are lid conditions but not the ptosis causes.
Myasthenia gravis, oculomotor nerve damage
Correct — the three, spanning neuromuscular junction, motor nerve and sympathetic chain. Damage to the sympathetic supply (Horner syndrome).

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: Where do tongue cancers usually appear, and in whom?
opts: On the dorsum, as smooth red patches, in females under thirty
Wrong site, wrong appearance and wrong group.
At the tip, as painful ulcers, in any age group
Painful ulcers at the tip are more typical of aphthous ulceration.
On the undersurface, as blue tortuous swellings
Those are varicose veins of the tongue, a benign finding.
On the lateral border or undersurface
Correct. Those two sites are exactly the ones a casual look misses, which is why the tongue is lifted and held. As indurated red or white lesions, in males over fifty.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: Which medication history should be taken specifically when a patient reports hearing loss?
opts: Oral contraceptives and hormone replacement

Aminoglycosides

Correct. All five are ototoxic, and all five are common enough that the question has to be asked by name rather than left to a general drug history. Aspirin, non-steroidal anti-inflammatories, quinine and furosemide.
Beta blockers, statins and proton pump inhibitors
None is listed as ototoxic here.
Inhaled corticosteroids and long-acting bronchodilators
Respiratory agents, not among the ototoxic drugs named.

A.io: c — Elements of the history that identify skin, hair and nail disorders
A.q: Generalised itching with no obvious skin lesion should prompt consideration of which causes?
opts: Contact dermatitis and scabies exclusively
Neither is on the list given for generalised itching without obvious cause.
Anxiety and stress, once organic causes have been excluded
The listed causes are organic rather than psychological.
Dry skin, ageing, pregnancy, uraemia, jaundice, lymphomas, leukaemias, drug reaction and lice
Correct — the list spans dermatological, systemic, malignant and infestational causes.
Dry skin and ageing only, since these account for nearly all cases
The differential is considerably broader and includes systemic disease.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: What are the pupil findings in Adie's tonic pupil?
opts: Small, unequal and irregular; no light reaction but constricts on accommodation
That is the Argyll Robertson pupil.
Small but briskly reactive, with ptosis and anhidrosis
That is Horner syndrome.
Dilated and fixed to both light and near, with ptosis and lateral deviation
That is an oculomotor nerve palsy.
Large, regular, usually unilateral
Correct — the near reaction being preserved but slow is the discriminator. Light reaction severely reduced and slowed or absent; near reaction present but very slow.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: What is the Rinne result in SENSORINEURAL hearing loss, and why is that counterintuitive?
opts: The result is unpredictable in sensorineural loss
The result is predictable: the normal ratio prevails.
Air conduction still greater than bone conduction
Correct. Rinne compares two routes to the same cochlea, so a damaged cochlea degrades both and leaves the ratio intact. The normal ratio prevails, because the damage impairs BOTH routes equally.
Bone conduction greater than air conduction, because the inner ear is damaged
That is the conductive pattern; a damaged inner ear does not favour the bone route.
Neither route is heard
Sensorineural loss reduces hearing but does not usually abolish it.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: Which two symptoms together suggest an allergic cause?
opts: Deep pain and photophobia
Deep pain points to acute narrow angle glaucoma.
Burning and purulent discharge
Purulent discharge suggests bacterial infection.
Foreign body sensation and reduced vision
Those point toward a corneal problem.
Itching and excessive tearing
Correct — it is these for allergy.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: A smooth, beefy red tongue points to which deficiency?
opts: Vitamin B12
Correct. The appearance is atrophic glossitis, and it earns a look for the rest of the deficiency picture.
Vitamin C
Vitamin C deficiency affects the gums rather than the tongue surface; the smooth beefy red tongue is attributed to B12.
Iron alone
Iron deficiency has its own oral signs, but the smooth beefy red tongue is attributed to vitamin B12.
Vitamin D
No such oral sign is given.

A.io: e — Clinical skills for a complete and focused skin examination
A.q: Which part of the hand should be used to assess skin temperature?
opts: The ulnar border
The ulnar border is used to assess vibration in some examinations, not temperature.
The dorsal aspect
Correct — the back of the hand is more sensitive to temperature than the palm.
The palmar aspect
The palm is used for texture and vibration rather than temperature.
The fingertips
Fingertips are best for fine tactile discrimination, not temperature.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: Eye pain ON EYE MOTION suggests what?
opts: Conjunctivitis
That gives grittiness.
Acute narrow angle glaucoma
That gives headache with eye pain.
Optic neuritis
Correct — the pairing for pain on movement.
Corneal abrasion
That hurts on blinking.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: Which headache patterns are EPISODIC, and which are UNILATERAL?
opts: Migraine and cluster are episodic; migraine and tension are unilateral
The pairings are swapped.
All three are episodic and all three unilateral
Tension headache is not described as unilateral.
Only cluster is episodic and only tension unilateral
Cluster headache is not the only episodic one, and tension headache is not described as unilateral.
Migraine and tension are episodic; migraine and cluster are unilateral
Correct. Migraine appears in both lists, which is why the two features have to be taken together rather than either alone.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: What does tracheal DEVIATION suggest?
opts: Thyroid nodules only
A mass may deviate the trachea, but the list given is broader.
Lymphadenopathy
Enlarged nodes do not typically deviate the trachea.
Ludwig's angina
That threatens the airway by swelling of the floor of the mouth rather than by deviating the trachea.
Masses, atelectasis or a large pneumothorax
Correct. Something is either pulling the trachea toward it or pushing it away.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: Eye pain with PHOTOPHOBIA suggests what?
opts: Inflammation of the iris
Correct — the pairing for photophobia.
Corneal abrasion
That is signalled by pain with blinking.
Temporal arteritis
That gives temporal pain.
Conjunctivitis
That gives a gritty feeling.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: What is trichiasis?
opts: Inward turning of the lower lid margin
That is entropion.
Outward turning of the lower lid margin
That is ectropion.
Drooping of the upper lid
That is ptosis.
Posteriorly misdirected eyelashes
Correct — the definition, listed alongside entropion and ectropion.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 35

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: VERTICAL diplopia — images on top of each other — points to a palsy of which cranial nerves?
opts: Third or sixth
That is the HORIZONTAL pattern.
Fourth or sixth
The third nerve features in both patterns.
Second or third
The second nerve is sensory, not motor.
Third or fourth
Correct, and this is one to memorise.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: How is the whispered voice test set up?
opts: Stand beside the patient and whisper into both ears at once
Each ear is tested separately, with the other occluded.
Stand two feet behind the patient, occlude the ear not being tested
Correct. Standing behind removes lip reading, and occluding the other ear stops it answering for the one under test. Whisper a three-item sequence twice.
Stand two feet in front of the patient so they can see your mouth
Seeing the mouth is exactly what the test has to prevent, which is why the examiner stands behind.
Stand across the room and speak at conversational volume
The test is a quiet whisper at two feet; conversational volume tests nothing.

A.io: c — Elements of the history that identify skin, hair and nail disorders
A.q: How should psychological stress be regarded in a patient with a skin disorder?
opts: It is the single commonest cause of chronic skin disease
Stress is explicitly described as seldom being the sole cause.
It has no demonstrable effect on the course of skin disease
It can exacerbate many dermatoses, so it is not irrelevant.
It should be raised only after organic causes have been excluded
Psychosocial factors are part of the routine history rather than a diagnosis of exclusion.
It is seldom the sole cause, but it can exacerbate many dermatoses
Correct — the distinction between causing and worsening is the point being made.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: Besides the whispered voice, which two bedside hearing screens are used?
opts: Weber and Rinne
These are the tuning fork tests, listed separately from the screens.
Finger rub and a watch
Correct — both are crude but immediately available, and both test whether any sound is heard at all.
Tuning fork and audiometry
The tuning fork tests distinguish the TYPE of loss; they are not screens for its presence, and audiometry is not a bedside screen.
Otoscopy and insufflation
Both examine the ear structurally rather than screening hearing.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: Submandibular swelling and erythema with cellulitis of the floor of the mouth. What is it, and what is the danger?
opts: A peritonsillar abscess — the danger is rupture
A peritonsillar abscess deviates one tonsil; it is not a floor-of-mouth cellulitis.
A submandibular stone — the danger is infection
A stone causes obstruction and swelling at meals, not spreading cellulitis.
Ludwig's angina — it is life threatening because of the AIRWAY
Correct. The swelling pushes the tongue and floor of mouth upward and back, and the airway is the reason this cannot wait.
Ludwig's angina — the danger is spread to the mediastinum only
Mediastinal spread can occur, but the stated danger is the airway.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: Which chain comes FIRST in the standard sequence for palpating the neck nodes?
opts: Preauricular

Correct. The sequence runs preauricular, postauricular, occipital, tonsillar, submandibular, submental, superficial cervical, posterior cervical, deep cervical, supraclavicular — following a route so none is missed.
Supraclavicular
That is last in the sequence.
Submental
It comes after the submandibular nodes.
Deep cervical
Near the end of the sequence.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: Which two conditions are associated with blepharitis?
opts: Graves disease and myasthenia gravis
Those relate to lid lag and ptosis.
Rheumatoid arthritis and lupus
Those are given for nodular episcleritis.
Bacterial infection and atopic dermatitis
Correct — the two associations to know.
Hypothyroidism and iron deficiency
Neither is given for blepharitis.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: In a trauma patient, what must NOT be done?
opts: Do not measure visual acuity
Acuity is still required.
Do not inspect the lids
Inspection is still required.
Do not take a history
The history is still required.
Do not palpate the globe
Correct — it is this critical in trauma.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 24

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: Watery or mucoid discharge suggests which conditions?
opts: Fungal infection
Not a category the material sorts by discharge.
Traumatic
Not sorted by discharge.
Allergic or viral
Correct — the pairing for watery and mucoid discharge.
Bacterial infection
That produces purulent discharge.
A.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 19

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: What is the Centor rule used for?
opts: Predicting which patients need tonsillectomy
Centor guides testing and treatment for an acute sore throat; the decision about tonsillectomy is a separate, longer-term one.
Deciding, from clinical features, how likely a sore throat is to be bacterial
Correct. It is a clinical prediction rule — it converts findings into a probability and a course of action.
Grading the severity of tonsillar enlargement
Tonsil size is not part of the rule. Centor converts four clinical features into a probability of bacterial infection.
Distinguishing peritonsillar abscess from tonsillitis
Asymmetry and trismus do that, not Centor.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: What does reduced mobility of the tympanic membrane on insufflation indicate?
opts: Sensorineural hearing loss
Insufflation assesses the middle ear mechanically and says nothing about the cochlea.
Effusion behind the membrane
Correct. The membrane cannot move if fluid is behind it or if it has been stiffened by previous disease. Or a thickened membrane.
Perforation of the membrane
A perforation prevents a pressure change being held at all, so the test cannot be interpreted that way.
Cerumen impaction in the canal
Wax blocks the view before it blocks the test.

A.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
A.q: A brown to black discoloration of the nail should raise concern for which diagnosis?
opts: Melanoma
Correct — pigmented change in a nail warrants the same concern as a pigmented skin lesion.
Pseudomonas infection
That produces a green nail.
Iron deficiency
That is associated with koilonychia rather than pigment change.
Psoriasis
Psoriasis produces pitting and onycholysis rather than brown-black pigment.

A.io: g — Documentation of a complete history and physical examination
A.q: How should physical examination findings be recorded in a written clinical note?
opts: Assign each system a numeric score on a standard scale
No scoring system of that kind is used.
Describe what was found, rather than writing normal, abnormal or unremarkable
Correct — a description communicates what was actually observed, where a label does not.
Use unremarkable wherever nothing is wrong, to keep the note concise
That is precisely the shortcut the guidance warns against.
Record only the abnormal findings and omit the normal ones entirely
Description is expected rather than omission.

A.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and colour
A.q: Which primary lesion usually precedes a crust?

A wheal is transient and resolves without crusting.
A nodule or tumor
These are solid masses and do not usually crust.
A vesicle, bulla or pustule
Correct — each of the three ruptures and leaves dried serum, blood and debris behind.
A macule or patch
Flat lesions have nothing to rupture and leave no crust.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: Purulent discharge suggests what?
opts: Bacterial infection
Correct — the pairing for purulent discharge.
Allergic conjunctivitis
That produces watery or mucoid discharge.
Viral conjunctivitis
That also produces watery or mucoid discharge.
Dry eye
That produces no discharge.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: Gradual, painless visual loss suggests what?
opts: Simple glaucoma or cataract
Correct — the gradual painless pair.
Acute narrow angle glaucoma
That is acute and painful.
Vitreous haemorrhage
That is acute.
Chemical exposure
That is acute and bilateral.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: How do you assess whether the eyes are truly protruding?
opts: Stand behind the seated patient and inspect from above
Correct — the technique Beck demonstrated and kept in scope. Drawing the lid slightly upward to compare the corneas against the lower lids.
Sit facing the patient and compare the two eyes directly
The material specifically asks you to look down from above.
Measure the distance from the lateral orbital angle with a ruler
That is the exophthalmometer measurement, which Beck said she would not test.
Palpate the globe to judge its forward position
Palpating the globe is contraindicated in trauma and is not the technique here.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: How is the auricle positioned to straighten the ear canal for otoscopy in an adult?
opts: Leave it undisturbed and advance the speculum slowly
Without straightening the canal the speculum meets the canal wall, which is both painful and uninformative.
Pull it up, back, and away from the head
Correct — all three directions. The canal is not straight, and the view is only as good as the alignment.
Pull it down and back
That is the manoeuvre for an infant, whose canal runs differently.
Press it forward against the cheek
This would close the canal rather than open it.

A.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
A.q: Which malignancy is the most frequent neoplasm occurring in patients with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome?
opts: Basal cell carcinoma
Basal cell carcinoma is common in the general population but is not the neoplasm associated with this condition.
Malignant melanoma
Melanoma is not the neoplasm most frequently associated with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome.
Squamous cell carcinoma
This arises on sun-exposed skin and is not the associated neoplasm.
Kaposi's sarcoma
Correct — the lesions start light coloured and coalesce into darker blue-purple macules, papules, nodules and plaques.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: How does the RATE of onset of visual impairment guide the differential?
opts: Rate of onset does not narrow the differential
It is it gives a clue to aetiology.
Rapid deterioration always means trauma
It is vascular causes.
Rapid deterioration suggests a vascular cause
Correct — the pairing of tempo with aetiology. Gradual loss suggests something like cataract.
Rapid deterioration suggests cataract; gradual loss suggests a vascular cause
This reverses the pairing.

A.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and colour
A.q: Psoriasis characteristically appears in which distribution?

Extensor

Flexor

Photodistributed
Skin cancers are the example given for sun-exposed distribution.

A.io: h — Involving the patient in healthcare communication
A.q: When a third party supplies the patient's responses during an assessed encounter, where should your attention stay?
opts: Divided evenly between the patient and the person answering
The instruction is unambiguous about interacting with the patient.
On the patient, interacting with the patient rather than the person supplying the answers
Correct, and it is stated emphatically. The encounter is with the patient even when the words come from elsewhere.
On whoever is supplying the answers, since that is the source of information
The instruction is the opposite: always look at and interact with the patient.
On the documentation form, so that responses are recorded accurately
Attention is meant to stay with the patient throughout.

A.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
A.q: In the melanoma warning signs, what does D stand for?
opts: Darkening of the surrounding skin
Colour variation within the lesion is what the letter C covers.
Diameter larger than six millimetres
Correct — six millimetres is roughly the diameter of a pencil eraser.
Depth of invasion into the dermis
Depth is determined on biopsy rather than by inspection.
Duration of more than six months
The letters describe appearance, not how long the lesion has been present.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: What is nystagmus, and when is a few beats normal?
opts: Fine rhythmic oscillation of the eyes
Correct — the definition and its normal exception. A few beats on LATERAL gaze is normal.
Misalignment of the visual axes — a few degrees is normal
That is strabismus.
Drooping of the upper lid — a few millimetres is normal
That is ptosis.
Unequal pupil size — a few millimetres is normal
That is anisocoria.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: Why might a patient with conductive hearing loss say they hear BETTER in a noisy room?
opts: The patient compensates by lip reading, which is easier in company
Lip reading may help in company, but the effect here is acoustic rather than behavioural.
The conductive block attenuates the background noise along with everything else
Correct. Others raise their voices over the noise while the patient's block filters the noise itself, so the speech-to-noise ratio improves.
Noise stimulates the cochlear hair cells directly
There is no such effect, and in conductive loss the cochlea was never the problem.
Conductive loss spares the high frequencies that carry noise
Conductive loss has little effect on which sounds are lost; it is the sensorineural pattern that takes the high registers.

A.io: a — Review the anatomical structure and function of the skin
A.q: Which glands become active during puberty and secrete pheromones?
opts: Apocrine glands
Correct. Their activation at puberty is what distinguishes them from eccrine glands.
Eccrine glands
Eccrine glands are functional from birth and secrete thermoregulatory sweat.
Sebaceous glands
Sebaceous glands surround hair follicles and secrete sebum.
Meibomian glands
These are the modified glands of the eyelid margin and are not the pheromone-secreting glands.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: Nasal polyps are associated with which conditions?
opts: Allergic rhinitis
Correct. Finding polyps should prompt asking about all five — cystic fibrosis especially in a younger patient. Aspirin sensitivity, asthma, chronic sinus infection and cystic fibrosis.
Hypertension, anticoagulation and atherosclerosis
Those are risk factors for posterior epistaxis, not polyps.
Smoking, alcohol and reflux
Those are listed in relation to hoarseness.
Diabetes, obesity and sleep apnoea
Diabetes, obesity and sleep apnoea are not the polyp associations; the five given run from allergy through to cystic fibrosis.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: Which part of the hand is used to palpate the lymph nodes of the neck?
opts: The fingertips of all four fingers
The technique specifies the pads of two fingers.
The thumb and index finger in a pincer grip
Shining the light into the nostril tests nothing; the maxillary sinus is lit from below the medial canthus.
The ulnar border of the hand
That is the otoscopy anchoring point, not a palpation surface.
The pads of the index and middle fingers
Correct. The pads are the most sensitive surface, and two fingers cover a node without rolling past it.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: Which two structures are commonly left unexamined?
opts: The eyelids and eyebrows
Not among the named omissions.
The lacrimal sac and puncta
Not among the named omissions.
The extraocular muscles
Movement testing is listed separately.
The cornea and the lens
Correct — 'failure to examine the cornea and lens' is on the list.

A.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
A.q: Alopecia areata is associated with which category of disease?
opts: Psychiatric disorders
Trichotillomania is the hair loss driven by an urge to pull.
Endocrine disorders of androgen excess
Androgen excess produces hirsutism and androgenic alopecia.
Autoimmune disorders
Correct — it is a chronic inflammatory disease of the hair follicles.
Fungal infections
Fungal infection of the scalp is tinea capitis, a separate diagnosis.

A.io: h — Involving the patient in healthcare communication
A.q: How should a student handle feedback that differs between facilitators?
opts: Disregard feedback that conflicts with earlier guidance
Feedback is to be accepted and acted upon.
Accept the constructive feedback and modify behaviour
Correct — the variation is anticipated rather than treated as a contradiction to be resolved. Recognising that different facilitators give different feedback.
Follow only the most senior facilitator's feedback
All constructive feedback is to be accepted and acted on.
Ask for a single standardised rubric to settle any disagreement
Adaptation is expected rather than standardisation.

A.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
A.q: What does the term hirsutism describe?
opts: Increased hair growth in women following a male pattern of distribution
Correct — the pattern of distribution, not simply the amount, defines the term.
Diffuse thinning of hair in women after menopause
That is a form of alopecia rather than hirsutism.
Loss of hair in multiple round patches
That describes alopecia areata.
Excessive fine hair covering the whole body in infancy
That is not the definition given.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
A.q: Which complaints fall in the URGENT group, seen by ophthalmology within a day or less?
opts: Dry eye and blepharitis
Those are routine.
Pinguecula and pterygium
Those are routine.
Acute glaucoma
Correct — the urgent list. Orbital cellulitis, corneal ulcer or abrasion, retinal detachment, macular oedema or haemorrhage, and hyphaema.
Sudden vision loss, chemical burns and globe rupture
Those are emergent, referred immediately.

A.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and colour
A.q: Which processes can convert a primary lesion into a secondary one?
opts: Only the passage of time, independent of any external factor
Specific processes are named rather than time alone.
Only secondary bacterial infection of the original lesion
Infection is not among the three processes listed.
Disease progression, treatment, and manipulation such as picking or scratching
Correct — the patient's own handling of a lesion is as capable of changing it as the disease itself.
Disease progression alone, since treatment does not alter lesion morphology
Treatment is explicitly listed as one of the causes.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: What does UNILATERAL nasal obstruction suggest?
opts: Allergic rhinitis
Allergic rhinitis affects the nose as a whole rather than one side.
Viral rhinitis
Viral rhinitis congests both sides. Unilateral obstruction is what points to a structural cause.
Rhinitis medicamentosa
Decongestant rebound affects both sides.
A foreign body
Correct. One-sided obstruction has a structural cause on that side, and the list runs from trivial to serious. A tumour, or a deviated septum.

A.io: e — Clinical skills for a complete and focused skin examination
A.q: A purple lesion does not fade when a glass slide is pressed against it. What does this indicate?
opts: Inadequate peripheral circulation
Cyanosis from poor circulation is not what the manoeuvre assesses.
Hemorrhage in the skin
Correct — blood outside the vessels cannot be displaced by pressure, which is why petechiae and purpura do not blanch.
Vascular engorgement
Engorged vessels empty under pressure and the colour fades.
An allergic reaction
Diascopy distinguishes hemorrhage from engorgement rather than identifying allergy.

A.io: e — Clinical skills for a complete and focused skin examination
A.q: You lift a fold of skin and release it, and the skin remains elevated. What does this indicate?
opts: Lichenification
Lichenification is thickening with accentuated skin lines from chronic irritation.
Scleroderma
This condition is not among those assessed by the turgor manoeuvre here.
Dehydration
Correct. Normal skin resumes its shape quickly; skin that stays tented has lost turgor.
Edema
Edema reduces mobility, meaning the skin will not lift easily in the first place.

A.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
A.q: Cracking and inflammation at the CORNERS of the mouth. What is this called?
opts: Angioedema
Angioedema is diffuse swelling, not cracking at the angles.

Whether the patient is being truthful about how often they bathe

Nutritional status through serum albumin and prealbumin levels

Whether the patient has access to running water at home
Housing is one small part of the social history rather than the assessment described.

An absent or closed ear canal

An extra accessory auricle

A small pit anterior to the tragus

B.q: Acute, unilateral and PAINFUL visual loss localises to where, and includes which causes?

Usually the lids — blepharitis and hordeolum

To look underneath for ulcers and lesions

To assess the fit of the denture itself

To allow the tongue blade to be inserted

opts: Pneumococcal

Hepatitis B
Not the immunisation it is.

Influenza
Not the immunisation it is here.

B.q: Which gland surrounds the hair follicle and keeps hair and skin moist?

Eccrine glands open onto the skin surface and secrete sweat for temperature control.
The apocrine gland
Apocrine glands secrete pheromones and switch on at puberty.
The sudoriferous gland
Sudoriferous is another name for the eccrine sweat gland.
The sebaceous gland
Correct — it secretes sebum directly into the follicle.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
B.q: Which features mark vertigo as CENTRAL rather than peripheral?

Ménière disease, also peripheral.
Hearing unaffected, tinnitus absent
Correct. The absence of ear symptoms alongside the presence of neurological ones is the pattern. Other brainstem deficits such as dysarthria, ataxia or crossed motor and sensory deficits.
Hearing impaired on one side with tinnitus present
That combination points peripheral — acoustic neuroma in particular.
Episodes lasting under a minute triggered by head position
That is benign positional vertigo, a peripheral cause.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
B.q: Which compensatory finding accompanies diplopia?
opts: A compensatory squint of one eye only
Not the finding it is.
Compensatory pupil dilation
Not a compensation for diplopia.
Compensatory tearing
Not what it is.
A compensatory head posture
Correct — patients tilt or turn to fuse the images.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
B.q: What does an acuity of 20/200 mean?

The notation describes acuity, not field.
At 20 feet the patient reads print that a person with normal vision could read at 200 feet
Correct — and the larger the second number, the worse the vision.
At 200 feet the patient reads print that a normal eye reads at 20 feet
This reverses the two distances.
The patient sees 20 per cent of normal at 200 feet
The notation is not a percentage.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
B.q: What are exostoses, and which type of hearing loss do they cause?

Correct. They narrow the canal mechanically, which is why the loss is conductive.
Benign bony growths on the ossicles, causing sensorineural loss
They are canal growths, and any canal problem produces conductive loss.
Malignant bone tumours of the temporal bone
Exostoses are described as benign bony growths. A malignant temporal bone tumour is a different problem entirely.
Cholesterol deposits in the middle ear
Cholesterol collections in the middle ear are cholesteatomas. Exostoses are bone, and they sit in the canal.

B.q: Which findings belong in an oral case presentation?

Pertinent negatives carry as much weight as positives in narrowing a differential.
Only the physical examination findings, since the history is documented separately
Both the history and the examination contribute to the presentation.
Pertinent positives and negatives from both the history and the physical examination
Correct. Choosing what counts as pertinent is the clinical reasoning being assessed.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
B.q: How is the tongue palpated?

That is bimanual palpation of the floor of the mouth, a separate manoeuvre.
Ask the patient to protrude the tongue and palpate the tip only

Use a tongue blade to depress and palpate through it
The blade is used to see the posterior pharynx, not to palpate the tongue.
Hold it with gauze in one hand and palpate with the other
Correct. Switching hands is what lets you reach both lateral borders properly, and the lateral border is where cancers sit. Then switch hands for the opposite side.

B.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and colour
B.q: What distinguishes a primary skin lesion from a secondary one?

The distinction is about the disease process, not about what the patient happened to notice.
A primary lesion forms first and results directly from the disease
Correct. Identifying the primary lesion is the key to interpreting and describing the eruption. While a secondary lesion is a change in that lesion over time.
A primary lesion is larger than one centimetre and a secondary lesion is smaller
Size distinguishes several individual lesions from one another but not the two categories.
A primary lesion is flat and a secondary lesion is elevated
Both categories contain flat and elevated lesions.

B.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
B.q: Dome-shaped, bright red to violet or black lesions also known as Campbell De Morgan spots are called what?
opts: Spider angiomas
Spider angiomas have radiating arms from a central macule.
Telangiectasias
Telangiectasias are fine irregular vessels.
Ecchymoses
An ecchymosis is a flat purple macule that fades over time.
Cherry angiomas
Correct — they may or may not blanch.

B.io: c — Elements of the history that identify skin, hair and nail disorders
B.q: Which historical factors should be explored for their relationship to the appearance of skin lesions?
opts: The patient's blood type and immunisation record
Neither is part of this line of questioning.
Season, travel, heat or cold, previous reactions, drugs and menses
Correct — each can be the trigger that explains the timing of an eruption.
Season and travel only, since the remainder are rarely relevant
The list is considerably broader than those two.
The patient's height, weight and body mass index
These are not among the relationships explored in a skin history.

B.io: Objective b — Terms describing lesion type (primary morphology), configuration (secondary morphology), texture, distribution and colour
B.q: What distinguishes a bulla from a vesicle?
opts: A bulla contains purulent material and a vesicle contains clear fluid
Purulent content defines a pustule.
A bulla is deeper in the dermis than a vesicle
Both are superficial elevations.
A bulla is solid and a vesicle is fluid-filled
Both are fluid-filled.
A bulla is larger than one centimetre and a vesicle is smaller
Correct — both are superficial elevations filled with fluid, and only size separates them.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
B.q: A patient reports ear pain but the ear itself looks entirely normal. Which structures should the history now cover?
opts: The thyroid gland and the trachea
Both belong to the neck examination, and neither is listed as a source of referred ear pain.
The parotid and submandibular glands
The salivary glands are not among the referred sources. The cranial nerves that carry the referral are V, VII, IX and X.
The temporomandibular joint
Correct. Ear pain is frequently referred, and these three are the usual sources. The first answer a patient gives is not the last question you ask. The teeth and the cervical spine.
The frontal and maxillary sinuses
Sinus tenderness is part of the nose examination. Referred otalgia comes from the joint, the teeth and the cervical spine.

Because they will be the ones making those dispositions

Because it closes the topic

Because it duplicates PD1 content

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
B.q: What is chemosis?

That is proptosis.
Outward turning of the lower eyelid
That is ectropion.
Swelling and inflammation of the conjunctiva
Correct — the definition.
Injection of the superficially visible vessels of the conjunctiva or sclera
That is hyperaemia.

B.q: In what order should an oral case presentation generally proceed?

The presentation builds toward the assessment rather than announcing it first.
Grouped by body system in alphabetical order
No such convention applies to case presentations.
Physical examination findings first, then the history that prompted them
The order should track how the encounter actually ran.
Mostly the order in which the history was obtained and the examination performed

B.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
B.q: A non-blanching reddish-purple macule measuring six millimetres is called what?
opts: Purpura
Correct — the three millimetre to one centimetre range defines purpura.
A petechia
A petechia is smaller than three millimetres.
An ecchymosis
An ecchymosis exceeds one centimetre.
A telangiectasia
A telangiectasia is a fine irregular vessel that blanches.

B.io: e — Clinical skills for a complete and focused skin examination
B.q: You lift a fold of skin and it does not lift with ease. What does reduced skin mobility suggest?
opts: Recent sun exposure
Sun exposure does not reduce skin mobility.
Edema
Correct — fluid within the tissue tethers the skin and reduces how freely it moves.
Dehydration
Dehydration is detected by turgor, where the skin remains elevated after being released.
Normal ageing of the skin
Ageing skin tends to move more freely rather than less.

B.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
B.q: Small depressions in the nail plate representing dystrophy of the plate are called what?
opts: Nail pitting
Correct — the pits are areas of small depressions in the nail plate.
Splinter hemorrhages
Splinter hemorrhages are hemorrhages of the distal capillary loop.
Beau's lines
Beau's lines are transverse depressions running across the nail.
Koilonychia
Koilonychia is a spoon-shaped concavity of the whole nail.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
B.q: What is the underlying lesion in Adie's tonic pupil?
opts: Degeneration of the ciliary ganglia and the postganglionic parasympathetic fibres
Correct — the stated pathology.
Interruption of the sympathetic supply
That is Horner syndrome.
Compression of the oculomotor nerve
That is a third nerve palsy.
Demyelination of the optic nerve
That produces an afferent defect.

B.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
B.q: Which finding defines a stage IV pressure ulcer?
opts: Non-blanching erythema over intact skin
That is stage I.
Full thickness skin loss with destruction of tissue, muscle and bone
Correct — involvement of muscle and bone is what separates stage IV from stage III.
Full thickness skin loss reaching but not penetrating muscle
That is stage III.
Partial thickness loss of the epidermis and dermis
That is stage II.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
B.q: Which size of speculum should be used, and why?
opts: A medium speculum regardless of canal size
The instruction is to match the canal and take the largest that fits.
Whichever gives the widest field of view, seal notwithstanding
Field of view is not the constraint — the seal is what the insufflation depends on.
The largest that will fit the canal
Correct. A small speculum is tempting but it leaks, and without a seal the pneumatic test tells you nothing. Because insufflation needs a proper seal.
The smallest available, to reduce discomfort
Comfort is not the criterion, and a small speculum cannot seal the canal.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
B.q: Why does the ABSENCE of cough count toward the Centor score rather than its presence?
opts: A cough points toward a viral cause
Correct. The rule is built to separate bacterial from viral pharyngitis, and cough is the most useful viral marker in the set. So its absence raises the probability of streptococcal infection.
Coughing masks tonsillar exudates on examination
Not the reasoning; the criterion is diagnostic, not technical.
A cough indicates the infection has spread to the lower airway
The criterion is about separating bacterial from viral pharyngitis, not about tracking spread to the lower airway.
Cough is a criterion only in children
The criterion applies as stated, and it is absence that scores.

B.io: e — Comprehensive versus focused history and examination
B.q: What distinguishes a focused encounter from a comprehensive one?
opts: The history and examination are both narrowed to what the presenting problem requires
Correct — a focused encounter is not a shorter version of everything, it is a targeted selection.
The examination is narrowed but the history remains complete
Both are narrowed in a focused encounter.
The history is narrowed but every system is still examined
The examination is focused as well.
The encounter is identical but documented more briefly
The difference is in what is gathered, not only in how it is written up.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
B.q: In unilateral CONDUCTIVE loss, which way does the Weber sound lateralise, and why?
opts: It does not lateralise in conductive loss
Lateralisation is precisely what the test detects, and conductive loss produces it.
It alternates between ears
Alternating lateralisation is not a recognised Weber result; the sound goes one way or stays midline.
To the IMPAIRED ear
Correct. The block screens out competing sound, leaving the bone-conducted tone unopposed in that ear. Because room noise is not well heard on that side so vibration is detected better.
To the GOOD ear, because the impaired ear transmits nothing
That is the sensorineural pattern. In conductive loss the cochlea is intact and hears the bone-conducted tone perfectly.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
B.q: A MULTINODULAR enlarged thyroid carries a risk of malignancy under what circumstance?
opts: When there is a family history
Correct — the multinodular gland is usually a metabolic process, and family history is what raises the concern.
Always, regardless of history
A multinodular gland is usually a metabolic process; it is a family history that raises the concern about malignancy.
Only if the gland is tender
Tenderness points to thyroiditis.
Only in patients under thirty
Age is not the stated qualifier.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
B.q: What is the normal appearance of the fundus and disc?
opts: White with absent tiny disc vessels
That is optic atrophy.
An enlarged cup with vessels sinking in around the disc
That is glaucomatous cupping.
Yellowish-orange to cream colour, small disc vessels, a sharp disc margin, and a cup located centrally or slightly temporal with a diameter normally less than half the disc
Correct — the full normal description, including the half-disc cup rule.
Pink with blurred margins and no visible cup
That is papilloedema.

Failing to diagnose a penetrated or ruptured globe
Correct — it is both the missed diagnosis and the pressure. Placing too much pressure on it, is a listed mistake.
Pressure is required to assess the depth of injury
The material warns against pressure.
Pressure is harmless once an anaesthetic is instilled

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
B.q: What are the pupil and lid findings in an oculomotor nerve palsy?
opts: A small pupil that reacts briskly, with ptosis and anhidrosis
That is Horner syndrome.
A large pupil with a slow but present near reaction
That is Adie's tonic pupil.
Small irregular pupils that accommodate but do not react
That is the Argyll Robertson pupil.
A dilated pupil fixed to both light and near effort
Correct — the full picture. With ptosis and lateral deviation of the eye almost always present.

Both always require emergency referral

This reverses the reading.

opts: Stage I
In stage I the skin is unbroken.
Stage III

Stage II

Stage IV

B.q: Vertigo comes on when the patient rolls onto one side in bed, lasts under a minute, and hearing is unaffected. Which is it?

Onset runs hours to as long as two weeks, not seconds.
Acoustic neuroma
Insidious, with impaired hearing on one side and tinnitus present.
Benign positional vertigo

Ménière disease

B.q: Why does a septal haematoma require URGENT drainage?

To prevent airway obstruction

To prevent secondary sinusitis

To prevent necrosis of the septal cartilage

B.q: On the red-eye chart, how is the PAIN of acute iritis described?

Mild discomfort rather than pain

Severe, aching, deep
That is glaucoma.
Absent
That is subconjunctival haemorrhage.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
B.q: The Weber test is done and the patient hears the tone only in the LEFT ear. Which ear has sensorineural hearing loss?
opts: The left
That would be true for a conductive loss, which lateralises TOWARD the affected side.
Neither — this is a normal result
A normal result is midline or equal in both ears.
Both
Weber evaluates unilateral loss; a bilateral symmetrical loss would not lateralise.
The right
Correct. Sensorineural loss lateralises AWAY from the damaged side, so hearing the tone on the left places the lesion on the right.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
B.q: Where do xanthelasma plaques sit, and what should they prompt?
opts: On the bulbar conjunctiva — consider ultraviolet exposure
That describes pinguecula.
Along the NASAL portions of one or both eyelids — consider lipid disorders
Correct — it is both the position and the inference.
Along the temporal portions of the lids — consider thyroid disease
It is the nasal portion and lipid disorders.
At the lid margin — consider bacterial infection
That describes a hordeolum.

B.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
B.q: Besides non-blanching erythema, which changes characterise a stage I pressure ulcer?
opts: Partial loss of the epidermis with a moist base
That is stage II.
Necrosis extending into subcutaneous tissue
That is stage III.
Changes in temperature
Correct — the area may be warm or cool, firm or boggy, and painful or itchy. Consistency, sensation and colour.
Changes in temperature alone
Consistency, sensation and colour changes are also described.

B.io: d — Physical examination findings of abnormal conditions of skin, hair and nails
B.q: Which of the following is a recognised cause of onycholysis?
opts: Prolonged immersion of the hands in water
Correct — local irritation from chemical exposure or prolonged immersion is one cause, alongside fungal infection, psoriasis, medications such as tetracycline, and trauma.
Iron deficiency producing a thinned nail plate
That mechanism produces koilonychia rather than separation of the plate.
Chronic hypoxia from lung disease
That produces clubbing.
A systemic illness three months previously
That produces Beau's lines.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
B.q: What are the four Centor criteria?
opts: Fever, tonsillar exudates, swollen anterior cervical adenopathy, and ABSENCE of cough
Correct. Three are things present and one is a thing absent, which is the part most often misremembered.
Fever, tonsillar exudates, swollen anterior cervical adenopathy, and PRESENCE of cough
Cough counts when it is ABSENT — a cough points away from streptococcal infection and toward a viral cause.
Fever, sore throat, headache and myalgia
A viral syndrome, not the Centor criteria.
Fever, trismus, uvular deviation and drooling
Those suggest a peritonsillar abscess rather than the scoring rule for pharyngitis.

B.io: c — Elements of the history that identify skin, hair and nail disorders
B.q: Which skin symptoms should be asked about when taking the history?
opts: Fever, chills and night sweats
These are systemic symptoms covered in the review of systems rather than skin symptoms.
Erythema, scaling and crusting
These are findings you observe rather than symptoms the patient reports.
Pruritus, pain and paresthesia
Correct — itch, pain and abnormal sensation are the three symptom categories.
Pruritus alone, since it is the commonest skin symptom
Pain and paresthesia are asked about alongside pruritus.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
B.q: Which part of the examiner's hand should rest against the patient during otoscopy, and what does it achieve?
opts: The ulnar aspect
Correct. The hand braces against the patient's head, so the instrument moves with the patient rather than into them. Which anchors the otoscope so a sudden movement does not drive it into the canal.
The palm, to steady the patient's head
The anchoring is of the instrument against the head, and it is the ulnar border of the hand that makes the contact.
The thumb, to hold the auricle in position
The other hand holds the auricle. The ulnar aspect of the otoscope hand makes the contact.
No part — the otoscope is held clear of the patient
Holding it clear is exactly what makes a sudden movement dangerous.

B.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced ENT History and Examination
B.q: What does a NORMAL lymph node feel like?
opts: Hard, fixed and irregular
Hard and fixed suggests malignancy.
Soft, tender and warm
Tenderness suggests inflammation.
Rubbery, matted and non-tender
Matting is an abnormal finding.
Round or ovoid
Correct. All four features matter, because each abnormal finding is a departure from one of them. Smooth, mobile and non-tender.

B.io: e — Clinical skills for a complete and focused skin examination
B.q: A patient has bluish discoloration of the fingers and toes with a normal oxygen level. What does peripheral cyanosis usually reflect?
